pos: adj. (filled full, lacking nothing; rendering Greek pleroo, participle, Hebrew tamim)
etymology: Latin complere, to fill up. Paul's Greek in Colossians is the participle of fill: the Colossians were filled-full in Christ, with no room for the additions being sold to them.
biblical_def: “For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily. And ye are complete in him, which is the head of all principality and power” (Col 2:9–10). Epaphras laboured in prayer for the same church, “that ye may stand perfect and complete in all the will of God” (Col 4:12). The feast of weeks: “seven sabbaths shall be complete” from the wave sheaf (Lev 23:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines complete as having no deficiency; perfect; finished, ended, concluded; and, as a verb, to finish, to make perfect.
webster_full: COMPLETE, a. Having no deficiency; perfect.
2. Finished; ended; concluded; as, the edifice is complete.
COMPLETE, v.t. To finish; to end; to perfect; to fulfil; to accomplish.
scriptures: Col 2:10
And ye are complete in him, which is the head of all principality and power:
Col 4:12
Epaphras, who is one of you, a servant of Christ, saluteth you, always labouring fervently for you in prayers, that ye may stand perfect and complete in all the will of God.
And ye shall count unto you from the morrow after the sabbath, from the day that ye brought the sheaf of the wave offering; seven sabbaths shall be complete:
corruption_summary: Christ is preached as the beginning to which something must be added, and Colossians says ye are complete in Him.
corruption_paragraphs: The Colossians were being told that Christ was not enough. Someone was offering them philosophy, the worship of angels, the rudiments of the world, ordinances of touch not, taste not, handle not — a fuller Christianity, a Christ plus — and Paul's answer is two verses long. In Him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily; and ye are complete in Him. A man in whom the whole fulness of God is has nothing to add, and a church filled full in Him has nothing to receive from the men at the door. Every Christ-plus since has been the Colossian heresy in new clothes: Christ plus the second blessing, Christ plus the sacrament rightly administered by the right hands, Christ plus the technique, Christ plus the tradition. Colossians 4:12 gives the word its other edge: complete in all the will of God, which is what Epaphras wrestled in prayer for — not more than Christ, but all of what Christ has.
roots_summary: Greek pleroo, perfect participle (G4137), filled full, complete; Hebrew tamim (H8549), whole, perfect, complete.
roots_lines: Greek pepleromenoi (G4137) — having been filled full, complete; Colossians 2:10, 4:12.
Hebrew tamim (H8549) — complete, whole; Leviticus 23:15, and of the lamb without blemish, Exodus 12:5.
usage: “Ye are complete in him” — nothing to receive from the men at the door.
“In him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily” — the ground of the completeness.
“Perfect and complete in all the will of God” — Epaphras's prayer.

pos: v. (grasped, laid hold of; summed up; measured; rendering Greek katalambano and anakephalaioo, Hebrew kul)
etymology: Latin comprehendere, to seize together. John's Greek is to lay hold of, whether by the mind or by the hand — the darkness neither understood the light nor overtook it.
biblical_def: “And the light shineth in darkness; and the darkness comprehended it not” (John 1:5). Paul on the commandments: “if there be any other commandment, it is briefly comprehended in this saying, namely, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself” (Rom 13:9). Isaiah on God: who hath “comprehended the dust of the earth in a measure, and weighed the mountains in scales” (Isa 40:12). And Paul's prayer: that ye “may be able to comprehend with all saints what is the breadth, and length, and depth, and height” (Eph 3:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines comprehend as to contain, to include; to imply; to understand, to take into the mind.
webster_full: COMPREHEND, v.t. To contain; to include; to comprise.
2. To imply; to contain or include by implication or construction.
3. To understand; to conceive; that is, to take, hold or contain in the mind; to possess or to have in idea.
scriptures: John 1:5
And the light shineth in darkness; and the darkness comprehended it not.
Rom 13:9

For this, Thou shalt not commit adultery, Thou shalt not kill, Thou shalt not steal, Thou shalt not bear false witness, Thou shalt not covet; and if there be any other commandment, it is briefly comprehended in this saying, namely, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.

Who hath measured the waters in the hollow of his hand, and meted out heaven with the span, and comprehended the dust of the earth in a measure, and weighed the mountains in scales, and the hills in a balance?
Eph 3:18
May be able to comprehend with all saints what is the breadth, and length, and depth, and height;
corruption_summary: John 1:5 is read as the world's failure to understand Jesus, and the Greek says the darkness could not overtake the light.
corruption_paragraphs: The darkness comprehended it not has become, in the liberal reading, a sad note about misunderstanding — the world did not grasp who Jesus was. The Greek verb is to seize, and John uses it in chapter 12 for darkness overtaking a man who walks at night. The darkness did not lay hold of the light: it neither understood it nor put it out, and the two senses are one claim, that the light shineth — present tense — and the darkness has never once got its hands on it. Golgotha was the darkness's best attempt. Romans 13:9 is the word's other misuse: the commandments are comprehended in love, and the antinomian reads it as replaced by love. The Greek is to sum up under one head, the word Paul uses in Ephesians 1:10 for gathering all things in Christ; the commandments are gathered under love, not dissolved in it, and Paul lists four of them by name in the same verse to make sure.
roots_summary: Greek katalambano (G2638), to seize, lay hold of, overtake, comprehend; anakephalaioo (G346), to sum up under one head; Hebrew kul (H3557), to contain, measure.
roots_lines: Greek katalambano (G2638) — to lay hold of, overtake, comprehend; John 1:5, 12:35, Ephesians 3:18, Philippians 3:12–13.
Greek anakephalaioo (G346) — to sum up, comprehend; Romans 13:9, Ephesians 1:10.
Hebrew kul (H3557) — to contain, comprehend in a measure; Isaiah 40:12.
usage: “The darkness comprehended it not” — neither understood nor overtook.
“Briefly comprehended in this saying” — gathered under love, not dissolved in it.
“Comprehended the dust of the earth in a measure” — Isaiah's God.

pos: v. (shut up together, enclosed; decided; rendering Greek sugkleio and krino)
etymology: Latin concludere, to shut up together. Paul's Greek is the fisherman's net closing — the same verb Luke uses for the draught of fishes — and God is the one who draws it.
biblical_def: “For God hath concluded them all in unbelief, that he might have mercy upon all” (Rom 11:32). “But the scripture hath concluded all under sin, that the promise by faith of Jesus Christ might be given to them that believe” (Gal 3:22). And the council's decision: “As touching the Gentiles which believe, we have written and concluded that they observe no such thing” (Act 21:25).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines conclude as to shut, to include; to close, to end; to determine, to decide; to infer.
webster_full: CONCLUDE, v.t. To shut.
2. To include; to comprehend.
3. To end; to finish.
4. To determine; to decide.
5. To infer, as a consequence; to deduce.
scriptures: For God hath concluded them all in unbelief, that he might have mercy upon all.
Gal 3:22
But the scripture hath concluded all under sin, that the promise by faith of Jesus Christ might be given to them that believe.

As touching the Gentiles which believe, we have written and concluded that they observe no such thing, save only that they keep themselves from things offered to idols, and from blood, and from strangled, and from fornication.
corruption_summary: Romans 11:32 is claimed for universalism, and the verse is about God shutting Jew and Gentile in the same prison so that the mercy would be His to give.
corruption_paragraphs: The universalist reads mercy upon all and stops. Paul's sentence begins with God shutting all up in unbelief — the Greek is a net drawn closed, or a prison door — and the two alls are the Jew and the Gentile whom the whole chapter has been comparing. Both were concluded in unbelief, the Gentile first and now the Jew, so that neither could claim mercy as a right and both would receive it as a gift. The verse is the strongest statement of sovereign mercy in the letter, not the weakest statement of its extent: the God who shuts the door is the God who opens it, and He opens it, the next verses say, according to judgments unsearchable and ways past finding out. Galatians 3:22 is the same net over the whole race. The scripture hath concluded all under sin — the law as a jailer, verse 23 says, shut up unto the faith which should afterward be revealed — and the purpose clause is the gospel: that the promise by faith of Jesus Christ might be given to them that believe.
roots_summary: Greek sugkleio (G4788), to shut up together, enclose; krino (G2919), to judge, decide.
roots_lines: Greek sugkleio (G4788) — to shut up together, conclude; Romans 11:32, Galatians 3:22–23, Luke 5:6 (inclosed).
Greek krino (G2919) — to judge, decide, conclude; Acts 21:25.
usage: “God hath concluded them all in unbelief, that he might have mercy upon all” — the door shut so that the opening is His.
“The scripture hath concluded all under sin” — the law as jailer, unto the faith.
“We have written and concluded” — the council's decision.

pos: v. and n. (to put off, linger; a putting off; rendering Hebrew achar and mahah, Greek chronizo, okneo, and anabole)
etymology: Old French delaier, to leave off. The Hebrew of Psalm 119:60 is to linger; the psalmist's boast is that he did not.
biblical_def: “I made haste, and delayed not to keep thy commandments” (Psa 119:60). The Law: “Thou shalt not delay to offer the first of thy ripe fruits” (Exo 22:29). At Sinai: “when the people saw that Moses delayed to come down out of the mount, the people gathered themselves together unto Aaron” (Exo 32:1), and the calf followed. The evil servant: “My lord delayeth his coming” (Mat 24:48). The disciples at Joppa sent to Peter “desiring him that he would not delay to come to them” (Act 9:38). Festus: “without any delay on the morrow I sat on the judgment seat” (Act 25:17).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines delay as to prolong the time of acting or proceeding; to put off; to defer; to retard; and, as a noun, a lingering, stay, stop.
webster_full: DELAY, v.t. To prolong the time of acting, or proceeding; to put off; to defer.
2. To retard; to stop, detain or hinder for a time.
DELAY, n. A lingering; stay; stop.
2. A putting off or deferring; procrastination.
scriptures: I made haste, and delayed not to keep thy commandments.
Exo 32:1

And when the people saw that Moses delayed to come down out of the mount, the people gathered themselves together unto Aaron, and said unto him, Up, make us gods, which shall go before us; for as for this Moses, the man that brought us up out of the land of Egypt, we wot not what is become of him.
But and if that evil servant shall say in his heart, My lord delayeth his coming;
Thou shalt not delay to offer the first of thy ripe fruits, and of thy liquors: the firstborn of thy sons shalt thou give unto me.
Act 9:38
And forasmuch as Lydda was nigh to Joppa, and the disciples had heard that Peter was there, they sent unto him two men, desiring him that he would not delay to come to them.
corruption_summary: Moses delayed forty days and Israel made a god, and the delay of the Lord's coming is still the hour in which men make theirs.
corruption_paragraphs: Exodus 32:1 is the anatomy of idolatry, and it begins with a delay. Moses was on the mountain receiving the pattern of the tabernacle, and the people, seeing that he delayed, made a calf to go before them; the interval between a promise and its performance is where the idols are made. Matthew 24:48 is the same interval in the New Testament: the evil servant's whole theology was my lord delayeth his coming, and everything he did followed from it. Peter says the delay is longsuffering; the servant read it as absence. Psalm 119:60 is the believer's tempo against both: I made haste, and delayed not — the commandments kept at once, because obedience postponed is a decision already made, and Exodus 22:29 gives the same rule to the firstfruits. What is God's is not delayed, and what is delayed was not really given.
roots_summary: Hebrew achar (H309), to tarry, delay; mahah (H4102), to linger; Greek chronizo (G5549), to take time, delay; okneo (G3635), to hesitate; anabole (G311), a putting off.
roots_lines: Hebrew achar, piel (H309) — to delay, tarry; Exodus 22:29, 32:1, Judges 5:28; mahah (H4102), Psalm 119:60, Genesis 19:16.
Greek chronizo (G5549) — to delay, tarry; Matthew 24:48, 25:5, Luke 12:45, Hebrews 10:37; okneo (G3635), Acts 9:38; anabole (G311), Acts 25:17.
usage: “When the people saw that Moses delayed… the people gathered themselves together unto Aaron” — where idols are made.
“My lord delayeth his coming” — the evil servant's whole theology.
“I made haste, and delayed not to keep thy commandments” — obedience at once.

pos: v. (caught, ensnared, held fast; rendering Greek enecho, empleko, and pagideuo, Hebrew buk)
etymology: En + tangle, of Scandinavian origin, seaweed that catches. Peter's Greek is to be woven in; the man entangled again is caught in a net he had once cut himself out of.
biblical_def: “Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage” (Gal 5:1). Of those who go back: “if after they have escaped the pollutions of the world through the knowledge of the Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, they are again entangled therein, and overcome, the latter end is worse with them than the beginning” (2Pe 2:20). The soldier: “No man that warreth entangleth himself with the affairs of this life” (2Ti 2:4). The Pharisees “took counsel how they might entangle him in his talk” (Mat 22:15). Pharaoh of Israel: “They are entangled in the land, the wilderness hath shut them in” (Exo 14:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines entangle as to twist or interweave in such a manner as not to be easily separated; to involve in any thing complicated and from which it is difficult to extricate one's self; to ensnare; to perplex.
webster_full: ENTANGLE, v.t. To twist or interweave in such a manner as not to be easily separated; to make confused or disordered; as, thread or silk is entangled.
2. To involve in any thing complicated, and from which it is difficult to extricate one's self.
3. To lose in a maze; to perplex; to bewilder.
4. To ensnare by captious questions; to catch; to perplex.
scriptures: Gal 5:1
Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage.

For if after they have escaped the pollutions of the world through the knowledge of the Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, they are again entangled therein, and overcome, the latter end is worse with them than the beginning.
No man that warreth entangleth himself with the affairs of this life; that he may please him who hath chosen him to be a soldier.
Then went the Pharisees, and took counsel how they might entangle him in his talk.
Exo 14:3
For Pharaoh will say of the children of Israel, They are entangled in the land, the wilderness hath shut them in.
corruption_summary: Legalism is preached as safety, and Paul calls it entanglement in a yoke Christ had already taken off.
corruption_paragraphs: Galatians 5:1 describes the peculiar sin of the freed. The Galatians had been made free by Christ, and they were letting themselves be entangled again — not in the sins they had left, but in a yoke: circumcision, days, the works of the law as the ground of standing. Legalism is not the opposite of licence; it is a second bondage that presents itself as safety, and Paul's word for a church going back under it is the word for a net. Second Peter 2:20 is the entanglement in the other direction, the man who escaped the pollutions of the world by knowing Christ and is woven back into them, and Peter's verdict is that his latter end is worse than his beginning, because the dog has returned to a vomit it had once left. Between the two verses the whole Christian life is bounded: not back under the law, and not back into the mire, and the standing fast is one act against both. Exodus 14:3 shows the last entanglement, the one Pharaoh saw: Israel shut in by the wilderness, entangled in the land — which was exactly where God had led them, so that the sea would open.
roots_summary: Greek enecho (G1758), to hold in, be entangled; empleko (G1707), to weave in, entangle; pagideuo (G3802), to snare; Hebrew buk (H943), to be perplexed, entangled.
roots_lines: Greek enecho (G1758) — to be held in, entangled; Galatians 5:1, Mark 6:19.
Greek empleko (G1707) — to be entangled, involved; 2 Timothy 2:4, 2 Peter 2:20; pagideuo (G3802), Matthew 22:15.
Hebrew buk (H943) — to be entangled, perplexed; Exodus 14:3, Joel 1:18, Esther 3:15.
usage: “Be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage” — the sin of the freed.
“They are again entangled therein, and overcome” — the net on the other side.
“They are entangled in the land, the wilderness hath shut them in” — Pharaoh's reading, and God's road.

pos: adv. (in plain and stated words; rendering Greek rhetos, and the Hebrew emphatic infinitive)
etymology: Latin expressus, pressed out, distinct. The Greek of 1 Timothy 4 is in so many words — the Spirit's warning about apostasy is not a hint.
biblical_def: “Now the Spirit speaketh expressly, that in the latter times some shall depart from the faith, giving heed to seducing spirits, and doctrines of devils” (1Ti 4:1). “The word of the LORD came expressly unto Ezekiel the priest, the son of Buzi, in the land of the Chaldeans by the river Chebar” (Eze 1:3). Jonathan to David: “If I expressly say unto the lad, Behold, the arrows are on this side of thee, take them; then come thou” (1Sa 20:21).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines expressly as in direct terms; plainly.
webster_full: EXPRESSLY, adv. In direct terms; plainly.
scriptures: Now the Spirit speaketh expressly, that in the latter times some shall depart from the faith, giving heed to seducing spirits, and doctrines of devils;
Eze 1:3
The word of the LORD came expressly unto Ezekiel the priest, the son of Buzi, in the land of the Chaldeans by the river Chebar; and the hand of the LORD was there upon him.

And, behold, I will send a lad, saying, Go, find out the arrows. If I expressly say unto the lad, Behold, the arrows are on this side of thee, take them; then come thou: for there is peace to thee, and no hurt; as the LORD liveth.
corruption_summary: Prophecy is treated as vague, and the Spirit spoke expressly about the apostasy and named its two marks.
corruption_paragraphs: First Timothy 4:1 is the Bible refusing to be vague. The Spirit speaketh expressly — in stated words, the Greek says — that some shall depart from the faith, and the verses that follow give the marks of the departure with a precision that has embarrassed one communion for fifteen centuries: forbidding to marry, and commanding to abstain from meats, which God hath created to be received with thanksgiving. The Reformers read the compulsory celibacy of the clergy and the fast-day laws in that verse and said so, and nothing in the text prevents it; what the text prevents is the claim that Scripture never speaks plainly about the future of the church. Ezekiel 1:3 is the same emphasis on the other side: the word came expressly — the Hebrew doubles the verb, came indeed — to a priest in exile who might have doubted whether the word could reach Chebar at all.
roots_summary: Greek rhetos (G4490), in express words, expressly; Hebrew hayo hayah (H1961 doubled), it surely came; amor omar (H559 doubled), I expressly say.
roots_lines: Greek rhetos (G4490) — expressly, in stated words; 1 Timothy 4:1 only.
Hebrew hayo hayah (H1961) — came expressly, came indeed; Ezekiel 1:3; amor omar (H559), 1 Samuel 20:21.
usage: “Now the Spirit speaketh expressly” — the apostasy foretold in stated words, with its marks.
“Forbidding to marry, and commanding to abstain from meats” — the marks the Reformers recognised.
“The word of the LORD came expressly unto Ezekiel” — came indeed, to Chebar.

pos: n. (the female of the domestic fowl; the Lord's figure for Himself over Jerusalem; rendering Greek ornis)
etymology: Old English henn. The Greek ornis is simply a bird; the Lord's image supplies the rest — wings spread over a brood, and the brood refusing.
biblical_def: “O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets, and stonest them which are sent unto thee, how often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not!” (Mat 23:37); Luke records the same lament on the road: “as a hen doth gather her brood under her wings, and ye would not!” (Luk 13:34).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines hen as the female of any kind of fowl; but it is particularly applied to the female of the domestic fowl of the gallinaceous kind.
webster_full: HEN, n. The female of any kind of fowl; but it is particularly applied to the female of the domestic fowl of the gallinaceous kind, or the female of the house-cock.
scriptures: O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets, and stonest them which are sent unto thee, how often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not!

O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, which killest the prophets, and stonest them that are sent unto thee; how often would I have gathered thy children together, as a hen doth gather her brood under her wings, and ye would not!
corruption_summary: The hen and the chickens is made the proof that grace can be resisted, and the ones who would not were the rulers who killed the prophets, standing between the hen and the brood.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 23:37 is the Arminian's favourite lament: the Lord would, and they would not, therefore the will of man is the deciding thing. Read the address. He is speaking to Jerusalem — the city that killeth the prophets and stoneth them which are sent — and the children He would have gathered are distinguished from the ye who would not. The rulers stood between the hen and the brood, as they had stood between the prophets and the people, and the verse is a lament over a leadership that hindered, not a confession that the Lord's gathering can be defeated by a chick. Every child He purposed to gather, He gathered; the ones who would not were the ones who shut up the kingdom against men and went not in themselves, four verses earlier. None of this makes the tears less real. The compassion is the compassion of God, who takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked, and the image is the oldest one in the Psalms — under the shadow of thy wings — offered by the One whose wings they were.
roots_lines: Greek ornis (G3733) — a bird, hen; Matthew 23:37, Luke 13:34 only; the wings of Psalm 17:8, 36:7, 91:4, Ruth 2:12.
usage: “Even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not!” — the rulers between the hen and the brood.
“Thou that killest the prophets” — the address that decides who would not.
“Under her wings” — the Psalms' oldest picture, offered by the One whose wings they were.

pos: v. (to strike out with the foot; of an ox, to kick against the goad; rendering Greek laktizo, Hebrew ba'at)
etymology: Middle English kiken, of uncertain origin. The Lord's proverb to Saul is the ox's: the goad is behind, the kick is against it, and the kick wounds the kicker.
biblical_def: The Lord to Saul: “I am Jesus whom thou persecutest: it is hard for thee to kick against the pricks” (Act 9:5; Act 26:14). Moses' song: “Jeshurun waxed fat, and kicked: thou art waxen fat, thou art grown thick, thou art covered with fatness; then he forsook God which made him” (Deu 32:15). God to Eli: “Wherefore kick ye at my sacrifice and at mine offering, which I have commanded in my habitation; and honourest thy sons above me” (1Sa 2:29).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines kick as to strike with the foot; to strike, thrust, or hit violently with the foot; and, intransitively, to practise striking with the foot, as a horse.
webster_full: KICK, v.t. To strike with the foot; as, a horse kicks a servant.
KICK, v.i. To practice striking with the foot or feet; as, a horse accustomed to kick.
2. To thrust out the foot or feet with violence, either in wantonness, resistance, anger or contempt.
scriptures: Act 9:5
And he said, Who art thou, Lord? And the Lord said, I am Jesus whom thou persecutest: it is hard for thee to kick against the pricks.
And when we were all fallen to the earth, I heard a voice speaking unto me, and saying in the Hebrew tongue, Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me? it is hard for thee to kick against the pricks.
But Jeshurun waxed fat, and kicked: thou art waxen fat, thou art grown thick, thou art covered with fatness; then he forsook God which made him, and lightly esteemed the Rock of his salvation.

Wherefore kick ye at my sacrifice and at mine offering, which I have commanded in my habitation; and honourest thy sons above me, to make yourselves fat with the chiefest of all the offerings of Israel my people?
corruption_summary: Saul's conversion is cited as the model of a free choice, and the Lord's own word for what Saul had been doing was kicking against a goad.
corruption_paragraphs: Acts 9:5 is the doctrine of effectual calling in a farmer's proverb. An ox under the goad kicks, and the kick drives the point deeper; the harder the beast resists the driver, the worse it wounds itself, and it goes where the driver meant it to go. Saul had been kicking — the goads were Stephen's face, the Scriptures he knew, the conscience that would not let the persecution be easy — and the light on the road was not an offer but an arrest. The man who describes his own conversion as a free decision has not read the Lord's description of Saul's. Deuteronomy 32:15 gives the other kick, the one that prosperity produces: Jeshurun waxed fat and kicked, and forsook God which made him, because a full people kicks at the hand that fills it. Eli's sons kicked at the sacrifice itself, and the word for the priests who despised the offering is the same word for the apostle who resisted the goad.
roots_summary: Greek laktizo (G2979), to kick, as an ox against the goad; Hebrew ba'at (H1163), to kick, trample.
roots_lines: Greek laktizo (G2979) — to kick; Acts 9:5, 26:14 only.
Hebrew ba'at (H1163) — to kick; Deuteronomy 32:15, 1 Samuel 2:29 only.
usage: “It is hard for thee to kick against the pricks” — effectual calling in a farmer's proverb.
“Jeshurun waxed fat, and kicked” — the kick prosperity produces.
“Wherefore kick ye at my sacrifice” — Eli's sons.

pos: n. (a judgment held; a view; in Kings, one of two sides halted between; rendering Hebrew dea and se'ippim)
etymology: Latin opinio, a supposing. Elihu's Hebrew is knowledge, and he calls it his; Elijah's is divided branches, and he asks how long.
biblical_def: Elijah on Carmel: “How long halt ye between two opinions? if the LORD be God, follow him: but if Baal, then follow him. And the people answered him not a word” (1Ki 18:21). Elihu, the young man who had waited: “I am young, and ye are very old; wherefore I was afraid, and durst not shew you mine opinion” (Job 32:6); “Hearken to me; I also will shew mine opinion” (Job 32:10); “I will answer also my part, I also will shew mine opinion” (Job 32:17).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines opinion as the judgment which the mind forms of any proposition, statement, theory, or event, the truth or falsehood of which is supported by a degree of evidence that renders it probable, but does not produce absolute knowledge or certainty.
webster_full: OPINION, n. The judgment which the mind forms of any proposition, statement, theory or event, the truth or falsehood of which is supported by a degree of evidence that renders it probable, but does not produce absolute knowledge or certainty.
2. The judgment or sentiments which the mind forms of persons or their qualities.
3. Settled judgment or persuasion; as religious opinions.
scriptures: And Elijah came unto all the people, and said, How long halt ye between two opinions? if the LORD be God, follow him: but if Baal, then follow him. And the people answered him not a word.
Job 32:6
And Elihu the son of Barachel the Buzite answered and said, I am young, and ye are very old; wherefore I was afraid, and durst not shew you mine opinion.
Therefore I said, Hearken to me; I also will shew mine opinion.
I said, I will answer also my part, I also will shew mine opinion.
corruption_summary: Faith has been reduced to an opinion, and Elijah refused to let Israel keep two.
corruption_paragraphs: The age calls religion an opinion and treats an opinion as private property, held or changed at pleasure and answerable to no one. Elijah's question on Carmel is the end of that comfort. How long halt ye between two opinions? — the Hebrew is two branches, a man with a foot on each — if the LORD be God, follow Him. The people answered not a word, because a religion of opinions has no answer to a demand for allegiance; it had never occurred to them that one of the two had to be false. Elihu's opinion is the other picture, and it is the better one: a young man who feared to speak before his elders, waited until they had exhausted themselves, and then said I also will shew mine opinion — and his opinion was truer than theirs, because great men are not always wise, and the inspiration of the Almighty giveth understanding. An opinion in Scripture is either a foot on a branch or a knowledge held under God; the modern sense, a preference nobody can question, is neither.
roots_summary: Hebrew dea (H1843), knowledge, opinion; se'ippim (H5587), divided opinions, branches.
roots_lines: Hebrew dea (H1843) — knowledge, opinion; Job 32:6, 32:10, 32:17, 36:3, 37:16.
Hebrew se'ippim (H5587) — divided thoughts, two opinions; 1 Kings 18:21; Psalm 119:113, “vain thoughts.”
usage: “How long halt ye between two opinions?” — a foot on each branch, and no answer.
“I was afraid, and durst not shew you mine opinion” — Elihu waiting for his elders.
“I also will shew mine opinion” — and it was truer than theirs.

pos: v. (to turn back, revoke, annul; rendering Hebrew shub, hiphil, to cause to return)
etymology: Latin revertere, to turn back. The Hebrew in every occurrence is to bring back — a blessing that cannot be called back, a decree that cannot be recalled.
biblical_def: Balaam to Balak: “Behold, I have received commandment to bless: and he hath blessed; and I cannot reverse it” (Num 23:20). Esther to the king: let it be written “to reverse the letters devised by Haman… which he wrote to destroy the Jews” (Est 8:5); and the king: “the writing which is written in the king's name, and sealed with the king's ring, may no man reverse” (Est 8:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines reverse as to turn upside down; to overturn; to change to the contrary; to repeal, annul, revoke; to bring back.
webster_full: REVERSE, v.t. To turn upside down; as, to reverse a pyramid.
2. To overturn; to subvert.
3. To turn back; to change to the contrary.
4. To repeal; to annul; to revoke; as, to reverse a judgment, sentence or decree.
scriptures: Behold, I have received commandment to bless: and he hath blessed; and I cannot reverse it.
Est 8:8

Write ye also for the Jews, as it liketh you, in the king's name, and seal it with the king's ring: for the writing which is written in the king's name, and sealed with the king's ring, may no man reverse.
Est 8:5

And said, If it please the king, and if I have found favour in his sight, and the thing seem right before the king, and I be pleasing in his eyes, let it be written to reverse the letters devised by Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite, which he wrote to destroy the Jews which are in all the king's provinces:
corruption_summary: Believers fear that a curse can undo a blessing, and Balaam, hired to curse, said he could not reverse what God had blessed.
corruption_paragraphs: Numbers 23:20 is the security of the blessed from the mouth of a man paid to curse them. Balaam had every motive to reverse the blessing — a king's reward, the king standing beside him — and he could not: he hath blessed, and I cannot reverse it. No enchantment against Jacob, no divination against Israel, and the reason is in the verse before: God is not a man, that He should lie, nor the son of man, that He should repent. The fear that a curse, a spell, an enemy's word, or the believer's own failure can call back what God has spoken over him is answered by a false prophet on a hill in Moab. Esther 8:8 is the human counterfeit: the law of the Medes and Persians that no man may reverse, so that Haman's decree stood and the only remedy was a second decree of self-defence. The irreversibility of God's blessing is a comfort; the irreversibility of a king's mistake is a tragedy He had to work around.
roots_summary: Hebrew shub, hiphil (H7725), to bring back, cause to return, reverse.
roots_lines: Hebrew lehashib (H7725) — to bring back, reverse; Numbers 23:20, Esther 8:5, 8:8, Isaiah 43:13, “who shall let it?”
usage: “He hath blessed; and I cannot reverse it” — the security of the blessed, from a man hired to curse.
“Sealed with the king's ring, may no man reverse” — the human counterfeit.
“To reverse the letters devised by Haman” — what Esther asked and could not have.
